title: Hybrid CPU-transplant fallback and sliding-window batch admission to avoid OOM during KV hot-spikes
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Intermittent OOMs occur on high-concurrency workloads when KV cache hot-key storms coincide with long sequences. Existing eviction and prefretch heuristics reduce frequency but still cause tail incidents. Goal: Provide an automatic, low-latency recovery path that preserves best-effort throughput and minimizes failed requests by combining (1) sliding-window batch admission that limits in-flight token memory growth, (2) KV shadowing to opportunistically checkpoint hot KV entries to host memory, and (3) a fast CPU-transplant fallback that executes a compact, quantized shard of the model on CPU for affected requests while the GPU recovers. This ticket designs and implements the control-plane and runtime hooks for the fallback, plus observability and canary rollout.
acceptance_criteria: When GPU free memory drops below configured headroom (default 12%), new incoming batches are admitted under a sliding-window that caps cumulative KV retention growth within the window.
KV hot keys are asynchronously checkpointed to host memory (shadow copies) with a configurable TTL; checkpointing reduces GPU-resident KV by >=40% on synthetic hot-storm tests.

If admission throttling + KV checkpointing do not restore headroom within 250ms for an affected instance, the runtime transparently routes the next 10% of matching requests to CPU-transplant execution with quantized 8-bit shards, with end-to-end latency increase <= 2x and success rate >= 95%.
Dashboard shows per-instance fallback count, average latency delta, and memory delta; alerts when fallback rate > 5% for > 5 minutes.
Unit, integration, and canary tests exist; rollback toggles disable CPU-transplant and KV-shadowing separately.
No customer data is persisted to disk during shadowing; KMS controls validated for any host-side caches.

design_notes: Rationale: existing techniques either shed tokens aggressively (hurting quality) or preemptively evict hot KV (hurting latency). The hybrid approach aims to keep most requests on GPU while providing a short-lived, quality-preserving CPU fallback for the small fraction that would otherwise fail.

CPU-transplant choice: 8-bit quantized shard is a pragmatic middle ground: smaller memory footprint, modest latency penalty, and reuses model code paths. We avoid full-model CPU fallbacks to keep recovery fast.
KV shadowing: implement as ring-buffered async writes to host pinned memory; entries tagged by request cohort to avoid cross-tenant leakage. TTL defaults to 30s but tunable per workload.
Admission window: sliding-window of 200ms with token-equivalent accounting; window size is tunable by tier (enterprise customers may increase headroom).

Routing policy: optimistic first: try admission + checkpoint; fallback only kicks in when both admission and checkpointing fail to release required headroom within threshold. Fallback is per-request and non-destructive (no model state mutation forwarded back to GPU).
open_risks: CPU fallback could increase load on control-plane if many instances fallback simultaneously—need throttles and circuit-breakers.
Quantization mismatch risk: outputs from 8-bit shard may have subtle quality differences; must validate against our eval prompts and include automatic regression alerts.
Host memory pressure: shadowing moves memory pressure to host; must ensure node-level limits and OOM guards for host side.
Security: ensure KV shadow does not write sensitive prompt tokens to persistent swap or disk; memory must be pinned and zeroed on eviction.

notes_for_reviewers: Please review the proposed headroom threshold (12%) and the 250ms recovery window — these values are conservative; ops may prefer tighter windows for higher SLA tiers.
Security review: confirm that host-side shadow copies meet our ephemeral memory rules and that pins/zeroing are sufficient.
Observability: ensure dashboard includes per-tenant fallback breakdown to detect noisy neighbors.
